Now I'm figuring out which dimension to distribute across for parallelism: fixing k, the update needs column k (M(a,k) for all a) and row k (M(k,b) for all b), and distributing by logical row a means accessing row k of M, which is strided in this column-major layout.\n\nChoosing to distribute by column b instead: each rank owns a block of columns, column k broadcasts contiguously (since storage index k*n+a is sequential for varying a), and row k values are local to each owned column. So the plan is to have the owner of column k broadcast it, then each rank updates its owned columns using that broadcast plus its local row-k entries — this keeps memory access efficient since owned columns form a contiguous block.\n\nI verify this is safe in-place: reads of column k and row k stay consistent during the update because M(k,k)=0 means those entries don't actually change, so there's no race condition. For GPU execution, the bottleneck becomes the per-iteration host-device transfer of the broadcast column — for n=4096 that adds up to a noticeable but manageable overhead, roughly 0.2 seconds total.\n\nI'm considering a pipelined approach where the owner of the next column broadcasts it early so other ranks can compute while waiting, though this adds complexity. Without guaranteed CUDA-aware MPI, I'll stick to staging through host memory: device-to-host copy of the column, broadcast, then host-to-device copy before the update kernel runs.\n\nI'm also weighing whether OpenMP should split work between CPU threads and the GPU for heterogeneous execution, but since a per-k broadcast sync is unavoidable anyway, the gains seem marginal for the added complexity—better to use OpenMP mainly for host-side tasks like parallel initialization and staging rather than splitting the core computation.\n\nThis adds real complexity since the owner of column k might have it GPU-resident, requiring a device-to-host copy before broadcasting and then a host-to-device copy back for GPU-resident ranks, which could eat into any gains from splitting work across host and device.\n\nGiven this, I think the more defensible hybrid design is to split each rank's local columns between CPU and GPU, with OpenMP handling the CPU-side portion and CUDA handling the GPU portion—say an 80/20 split favoring the GPU since it's likely much faster, though the exact fraction is uncertain without benchmarking the specific hardware.\n\nActually, conditionally enabling OpenMP for zero columns doesn't make sense, so I need to reconsider the hybrid split: CPU-owned columns live in host memory while GPU-owned columns stay on device, with the broadcast buffer letting whoever needs column k copy it from wherever it resides. To keep this manageable, I'll just keep the entire local block mirrored on host memory as well.\n\nPer rank, I'm sketching out the concrete flow: separate device buffers for the GPU-owned columns and host arrays for the CPU-owned columns, with each iteration requiring the owner of column k to pull it into a shared buffer — either via a device-to-host copy if it lives on GPU, or a direct host copy if it's already there — before broadcasting that column to all ranks via MPI, making sure stream synchronization happens correctly beforehand.\n\nAfter the broadcast, I copy the column host-to-device asynchronously, then launch the GPU kernel for the gpu-owned columns while simultaneously running an OpenMP loop over the CPU-owned columns, syncing streams before the next iteration begins so the overlap works cleanly. The path matrix mirrors dist but never gets communicated, only gathered at the end — and for final output I need to collect both GPU and CPU portions into a contiguous per-rank buffer before doing an MPI Gatherv to assemble the full matrix on rank 0.\n\nI'm settling on making the host-side array the canonical storage for the CPU-owned columns, D2H copying the GPU-owned columns into the same buffer, then using Gatherv with column-major contiguous blocks placed at the right displacement in the global array. The path array gets the same treatment even though it's never actually printed, just to preserve the program's original semantics.\n\nFor the kernel update, each thread handles one (row, column) pair, reading a coalesced column element and a broadcast row element to apply the min-plus relaxation for the current pivot k.\n\nBut I realize the row k value itself lives in the same array being written, which risks a technical data race even though the written value is unchanged. I'm now also noticing row k of the matrix is distributed across ranks in the column-sharded layout, so I need a separate buffer to hold that row before using it.\n\nSo the plan: a small gather kernel copies dist[b*n+k] into a local rowBuf before the update, avoiding any races, and the update kernel itself only reads and writes dist[b*n+a] per thread, keeping memory access clean. I'm also estimating the total memory traffic for the whole algorithm, since it's purely memory-bound with roughly n³ element touches across all iterations.\n\nI'm weighing blocked (tiled) Floyd-Warshall as a way to cut that memory traffic, but it's a much bigger rewrite, and I need to confirm it would still produce identical path tie-breaking — since standard FW records the first strictly-improving k in increasing order, and blocked FW processes k in the same increasing order within each block, the results should match as long as the block decomposition preserves that per-pair k ordering.\n\nThis is too subtle a correctness risk to pursue, so I'll stick with the exact standard k-by-k algorithm to guarantee equivalence, and instead focus optimization efforts on memory bandwidth — fusing the read/compute/write of dist and path into a single kernel pass that only writes path when there's a strict improvement.\n\nThat fusion approach gets too complicated since row k+1 values are also locally updated — not worth it. The split fraction needs to be tiny and hardware-dependent, so the honest approach is to measure each device's throughput at startup and calibrate the split dynamically.\n\nI'm also weighing where OpenMP actually helps without adding risk: parallelizing path initialization and giving the CPU a small, fixed share of host-side column updates seems like the safest unconditional use, avoiding complex adaptive rebalancing or new environment variables that could count as scope creep. Each iteration k, the\n//     owner of column k broadcasts it; every rank then updates its own columns.\n//     Row k of the local block is always local, so no other communication is\n//     needed.\n//   * CUDA: each rank drives one GPU (local rank modulo device count) and\n//     updates the leading part of its local block with a 2D kernel.\n//   * OpenMP: the trailing part of the local block is updated by host threads\n//     concurrently with the GPU kernel. Path initialization and the host-side\n//     staging also run multithreaded.\n//\n// Semantics match the sequential algorithm exactly: for each k, column k and\n// row k are invariant (the diagonal is zero), so every element update reads the\n// same operands as the in-place sequential loop, and k is processed in order,\n// so path tie-breaking (strict '<') is identical.\n\n#include <mpi.h>\n#include <cuda_runtime.h>\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include \"../common/results_output.hpp\"\n\nconstexpr unsigned int INF = 1000000000;\nconstexpr unsigned int MAX_DISTANCE = 200;\n\n// Fraction of each rank's local columns updated by OpenMP host threads.\n// The remaining columns are updated on the rank's GPU.\nconstexpr double CPU_COLUMN_SHARE = 0.02;\n\nconstexpr unsigned int CUDA_BLOCK_SIZE = 256;\nconstexpr unsigned int CUDA_MAX_GRID_Y = 65535;\n\n#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                          \\\n    do {                                                                          \\\n        cudaError_t err_ = (call);                                                \\\n        if (err_ != cudaSuccess) {                                                \\\n            fprintf(stderr, \"CUDA error at %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__,      \\\n                    cudaGetErrorString(err_));                                    \\\n            MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);                                         \\\n        }                                                                         \\\n    } while (0)\n\n// Index calculation for flattened 2D array\ninline constexpr size_t idx2(const size_t i, const size_t j, const size_t n) noexcept {\n    return j * n + i;\n}\n\nvoid initializeDistanceMatrix(std::vector<unsigned int>& dist, const size_t numNodes, \n                              const unsigned int rangeMin, const unsigned int rangeMax) {\n    unsigned int seed = 42;\n    const double range = static_cast<double>(rangeMax - rangeMin) + 1.0;\n    \n    for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes * numNodes; ++i) {\n        dist[i] = rangeMin + (unsigned int)(range * rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX);\n    }\n    \n    // Set diagonal to zero (distance from node to itself is 0)\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n        dist[idx2(i, i, numNodes)] = 0;\n    }\n}\n\n// Initializes the path entries for the local columns [firstCol, firstCol + numCols).\n// The path value of element (a, b) is b in the original initialization.\nvoid initializeLocalPathMatrix(std::vector<unsigned int>& path, const size_t numNodes,\n                               const size_t firstCol, const size_t numCols) {\n    #pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)\n    for (long long j = 0; j < static_cast<long long>(numCols); ++j) {\n        unsigned int* column = path.data() + static_cast<size_t>(j) * numNodes;\n        const unsigned int value = static_cast<unsigned int>(firstCol + static_cast<size_t>(j));\n        std::fill(column, column + numNodes, value);\n    }\n}\n\n// Device kernel: one step k of Floyd-Warshall on the GPU-resident columns.\n// Element (a, b) of the local block lives at b * n + a.\n__global__ void floydWarshallStepGpu(unsigned int* __restrict__ dist,\n                                     unsigned int* __restrict__ path,\n                                     const unsigned int* __restrict__ colK,\n                                     const unsigned int* __restrict__ rowK,\n                                     const size_t n, const size_t gpuCols,\n                                     const unsigned int k) {\n    const size_t a = static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;\n    if (a >= n) {\n        return;\n    }\n    for (size_t b = blockIdx.y; b < gpuCols; b += gridDim.y) {\n        const size_t idx = b * n + a;\n        const unsigned int distIJ = dist[idx];\n        const unsigned int newDist = colK[a] + rowK[b];\n        if (newDist < distIJ) {\n            dist[idx] = newDist;\n            path[idx] = k;\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n// Host update of one Floyd-Warshall step on the CPU-resident columns.\n// `dist`/`path` point to the first CPU column; `rowK[b]` holds M(k, b).\nvoid floydWarshallStepCpu(unsigned int* dist, unsigned int* path,\n                          const unsigned int* colK, const unsigned int* rowK,\n                          const size_t n, const size_t numCols, const unsigned int k) {\n    #pragma omp parallel for collapse(2) schedule(static)\n    for (long long b = 0; b < static_cast<long long>(numCols); ++b) {\n        for (long long a = 0; a < static_cast<long long>(n); ++a) {\n            const size_t idx = static_cast<size_t>(b) * n + static_cast<size_t>(a);\n            const unsigned int distIJ = dist[idx];\n            const unsigned int newDist = colK[a] + rowK[b];\n            if (newDist < distIJ) {\n                dist[idx] = newDist;\n                path[idx] = k;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\nbool validateResult(const std::vector<unsigned int>& dist, const size_t numNodes) {\n    // Basic sanity checks\n    \n    // 1. Diagonal should be zero\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n        if (dist[idx2(i, i, numNodes)] != 0) {\n            printf(\"Validation failed: diagonal element [%zu,%zu] is not zero\\n\", i, i);\n            return false;\n        }\n    }\n    \n    // 2. Triangle inequality: dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] >= dist[i][j]\n    // Check a sample of paths to avoid O(n^3) validation time\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < std::min(numNodes, static_cast<size_t>(10)); ++i) {\n        for (size_t j = 0; j < std::min(numNodes, static_cast<size_t>(10)); ++j) {\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < numNodes; ++k) {\n                const unsigned int distIJ = dist[idx2(j, i, numNodes)];\n                const unsigned int distIK = dist[idx2(k, i, numNodes)];\n                const unsigned int distKJ = dist[idx2(j, k, numNodes)];\n                \n                // Check for overflow before addition\n                if (distIK < INF && distKJ < INF) {\n                    if (distIK + distKJ < distIJ) {\n                        printf(\"Validation failed: triangle inequality violated at [%zu,%zu,%zu]\\n\", \n                               i, j, k);\n                        return false;\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    \n    return true;\n}\n\nvoid printUsage(const char* progName) {\n    printf(\"Usage: %s [options]\\n\", progName);\n    printf(\"Options:\\n\");\n    printf(\"  -n <num>     Number of nodes in the graph (default: 512)\\n\");\n    printf(\"  -v           Enable validation\\n\");\n    printf(\"  -r           Print results for external validation\\n\");\n    printf(\"  -h           Show this help message\\n\");\n}\n\nint main(int argc, char** argv) {\n    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);\n\n    int rank = 0;\n    int numRanks = 1;\n    MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);\n    MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &numRanks);\n    const bool root = (rank == 0);\n    const MPI_Comm comm = MPI_COMM_WORLD;\n\n    size_t numNodes = 512;\n    bool validate = false;\n    bool printResults = false;\n    \n    // Parse command line arguments\n    for (int i = 1; i < argc; ++i) {\n        if (strcmp(argv[i], \"-n\") == 0 && i + 1 < argc) {\n            numNodes = atoi(argv[++i]);\n        } else if (strcmp(argv[i], \"-v\") == 0) {\n            validate = true;\n        } else if (strcmp(argv[i], \"-r\") == 0) {\n            printResults = true;\n        } else if (strcmp(argv[i], \"-h\") == 0) {\n            if (root) printUsage(argv[0]);\n            MPI_Finalize();\n            return 0;\n        } else {\n            if (root) {\n                printf(\"Unknown option: %s\\n\", argv[i]);\n                printUsage(argv[0]);\n            }\n            MPI_Finalize();\n            return 1;\n        }\n    }\n    \n    if (root) {\n        printf(\"Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Path Benchmark\\n\");\n        printf(\"Number of nodes: %zu\\n\", numNodes);\n        printf(\"Validation: %s\\n\", validate ? \"enabled\" : \"disabled\");\n        printf(\"Initializing graph...\\n\");\n    }\n\n    // Bind each rank to a GPU, round-robin over the GPUs on its node.\n    MPI_Comm nodeComm;\n    MPI_Comm_split_type(comm, MPI_COMM_TYPE_SHARED, rank, MPI_INFO_NULL, &nodeComm);\n    int localRank = 0;\n    MPI_Comm_rank(nodeComm, &localRank);\n    MPI_Comm_free(&nodeComm);\n\n    int deviceCount = 0;\n    CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDeviceCount(&deviceCount));\n    if (deviceCount == 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"Rank %d: no CUDA devices available\\n\", rank);\n        MPI_Abort(comm, 1);\n    }\n    CUDA_CHECK(cudaSetDevice(localRank % deviceCount));\n\n    // Column-block distribution: rank r owns columns [colStart(r), colStart(r) + colCount(r)).\n    const size_t n = numNodes;\n    const size_t baseCols = n / static_cast<size_t>(numRanks);\n    const size_t extraCols = n % static_cast<size_t>(numRanks);\n    auto colCount = [&](int r) -> size_t {\n        return baseCols + (static_cast<size_t>(r) < extraCols ? 1 : 0);\n    };\n    auto colStart = [&](int r) -> size_t {\n        return static_cast<size_t>(r) * baseCols + std::min(static_cast<size_t>(r), extraCols);\n    };\n    auto ownerOf = [&](size_t k) -> int {\n        for (int r = 0; r < numRanks; ++r) {\n            if (k < colStart(r) + colCount(r)) return r;\n        }\n        return numRanks - 1;\n    };\n\n    const size_t myCols = colCount(rank);\n    const size_t myStart = colStart(rank);\n    const size_t cpuCols = static_cast<size_t>(static_cast<double>(myCols) * CPU_COLUMN_SHARE);\n    const That seems off given the CPU workload per rank is tiny (just 10 columns with 256 threads), so I suspect the bottleneck is elsewhere, maybe on the GPU side of the k-loop.\n\nDoing the math on element throughput, the GPU kernel work alone should only take tens of microseconds per k, nowhere near what's observed at n=2048 where np=1 takes 9s versus np=4 at 159ms. The CPU share calculation doesn't explain it either — 41 columns across 256 threads should finish in under a microsecond, not milliseconds. I want to isolate this by rerunning np=1 with the CPU column share set to zero to see if the slowdown disappears.\n\nLooking more closely, I suspect the culprit is the cudaMemcpy2DAsync call copying from dDist — with a width of only 4 bytes per row and 2008 rows, this could be issuing thousands of tiny strided transfers instead of one efficient bulk copy, which would explain why the per-rank cost scales so poorly as the row count grows for np=1 versus the smaller row count per GPU at np=4.\n\nSo instead of relying on that memcpy2D, I should replace it with a small dedicated gather kernel that pulls the k-th row values directly from the distance matrix into a compact buffer, avoiding the inefficient strided DMA pattern entirely.\n\n","time":{"start":1793010344187,"end":1793010353778},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793010435530,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"id":"prt_177bfe9d3001kOtb3J0JzAL9LY","messageID":"msg_177bfe442001dV4Vlw5Wo67C1i","sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","type":"reasoning","text":"The CPU side is actually the bottleneck despite its small reported share—floydWarshallStepCpu with 41 columns running under OpenMP across 256 threads seems to be paying huge per-iteration overhead, possibly from thread creation costs each loop plus GPU sync waits, which would explain the roughly 4.4ms per iteration across 2048 iterations.\n\nI suspect the real issue is that 256 OMP threads busy-spin after each parallel region (GOMP's spin-wait policy), hogging all CPU cores and starving the CUDA driver's worker threads—so the GPU kernels run fine, but the host-side stream sync and launch calls get stalled waiting for a free core.\n\nSo the fix is to cap the OMP thread count to something small, like 4-16 threads, since the CPU-side work is tiny anyway (handling only ~2% of columns). I want to experiment with explicit thread caps—maybe scaling with online CPUs divided by local rank count—and test a few values like 4, 8, 16, 32 to see what avoids the spin-wait starvation while still getting enough parallelism.\n\n","time":{"start":1793010428371,"end":1793010435476},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

Estimating the raw compute cost at only ~43ms per thread suggests the measured 360ms overhead is mostly sync overhead from the GPU/CPU coupling rather than actual computation.\n\nGPU kernels run roughly 50us per k while the CPU chunk takes similar time, plus fork/join overhead adds another 10-50us each cycle. That tells me the current 2% CPU share isn't properly balanced against the GPU/CPU throughput ratio—a correct split would need to account for relative hardware speeds, which is highly hardware-specific. The honest conclusion for this setup: GPU-only outperforms the hybrid split at the tested configuration, since the balance would need careful tuning to actually pay off.\n\nI still need to use OpenMP meaningfully though. I could try sweeping smaller CPU shares (0.005-0.01) with 4-8 threads to see if there's a sweet spot, but the real issue seems to be that the CPU loop itself is inefficient—220us for 21k elements per thread works out to roughly 10ns per element, which is too slow. That's likely due to the collapsed loop structure with branching and long long index variables that need optimizing.\n\n","time":{"start":1793010485716,"end":1793010494484},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793010589191,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"id":"prt_177c237a4001Bg3d4bpCho0epC","messageID":"msg_177c231bd0013SRbSrvnX69lr2","sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","type":"reasoning","text":"I notice with np=4, the CPU share barely matters since GPU work dominates, but with np=1 it really hurts — each additional slice of columns adds roughly 100 microseconds, so going from a 0.002 to 0.005 share adds hundreds of milliseconds overall.\n\nThat works out to something like 25 microseconds per column, or ~12ns per element, which is way too slow for simple CPU work. I'm wondering if it's the OpenMP fork/join overhead, memory access patterns in the hDist vector, or contention between CUDA's stream synchronization spin-waiting and the OpenMP threads — though with 256 cores available, contention seems unlikely. The real question is whether the CPU work is actually overlapping with the async GPU kernel launch as intended, since the whole point is that per-iteration time should be the max of the GPU and CPU durations, not their sum.\n\nWorking through the numbers: with roughly 50 microseconds per GPU iteration but over 100 microseconds needed for just 10 CPU columns across 8 threads, that's suspiciously slow for data that should fit in L2 cache after the first pass. I'm starting to suspect NUMA effects since the data was written by a single thread during Scatterv, or possibly a thread affinity issue where OMP threads are all pinned to one core due to inherited process affinity settings.\n\nThat's the likely culprit — OpenMPI binds processes to a single core by default when np is 2 or fewer, so all 8 OMP threads get time-sliced on one core instead of spreading out, which would explain the contention with the CUDA thread too. I should suggest running with `--bind-to none` to test this theory, since the program itself shouldn't be messing with scheduling affinity directly.\n\n","time":{"start":1793010579364,"end":1793010589111},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793010641492,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"id":"prt_177c2f3aa001ufWAknGSY4S8hv","messageID":"msg_177c2ea6a001U17nj47hH10O6p","sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","type":"reasoning","text":"Binding turns out to be the real culprit—disabling it drops the time from 360ms to 129ms, though there's still ~30ms overhead with 10 columns. But since production code can't control mpirun flags and the benchmark will likely run with default settings, I'm stuck thinking about how to make this robust without being able to easily rebind inside processes.\n\nOne option is calling sched_setaffinity to free up all CPUs before spawning the OpenMP team, but that risks contention since every rank would then compete for all cores. A cleaner approach is giving each rank a disjoint slice of cores based on its local rank index, sized by the number of local ranks, which yields deterministic hybrid placement regardless of how mpirun binds things—though it does override whatever the launcher (like Slurm) set up. A gentler middle ground is to just read the process's current affinity mask and divide those cores among local ranks, respecting any cgroup-based restriction while still working sensibly if mpirun has already bound things.\n\nLooking at the actual numbers though: with np=1 bound to a single core, I'd end up with just one OpenMP thread, which is slow but honest—I'd just need to flag `--bind-to none` in the writeup. On the CPU share question, the measurements are telling: 0% share gives 100ms while 0.5% share bumps it to 129ms at np=1 with 8 threads, so there's no actual gain from reserving CPU share on this hardware—it's a net loss, suggesting it should default to zero unless there's a specific reason to do otherwise.\n\nBut the requirement to use OpenMP unconditionally complicates this. If CPU share is zero, the CPU-side compute path never runs, making OpenMP look like window dressing. I'm weighing whether a small nonzero share (like 0.5%) is worth the tradeoff—it costs little when running 4 ranks per node (92 vs 105ms, within noise) but costs ~30% when there's only one GPU and one rank, which is a bad deal in that case. Making the share conditional on thread count or GPU count would violate the \"unconditional\" requirement, so I'm leaning toward just picking a small fixed value like 1/256 as a compromise.\n\nWorking through the math: GPU throughput is roughly 84 elements/ns while 8 CPU threads manage about 1 elem/ns, so a balanced share would be around 1-1.2%, but at smaller n the fork/join overhead (5-10us) plus stream sync dominates and erases any savings. At larger n like 4096, GPU work per step balloons to ~200us while CPU work stays near 10-20us, so the overhead gets hidden and the CPU share becomes nearly free. I want to run a quick sweep at n=4096 with np=1 and np=4, testing share values of 0, 0.005, and 0.01 with 8 threads to settle on a final number.\n\n","time":{"start":1793010627498,"end":1793010641426},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793011107425,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"id":"prt_177ca2bb80011CXzQwyKo093hP","messageID":"msg_177ca23ee001GMs5pGlhtkNGmp","sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm seeing that the default binding with np=1 pins to a single core, limiting it to one thread of CPU share — that's a real bottleneck at n=4096, since it caps throughput around 41 columns per unit time on a single thread. This binding behavior is a hazard worth flagging.\n\nA simpler, more robust fix is to scale the CPU share by available thread count rather than a fixed percentage: I'll compute hostThreads via omp_get_max_threads() and set cpuCols proportionally, something like 0.25% per thread, so 8 threads yields roughly 2% CPU share while 1 thread yields 0.25%. This keeps the tuning hardware-aware without overengineering it.\n\nBased on earlier measurements—1% at 8 threads worked well (529 vs 572), while 2% caused overhead issues at different configurations—I'll settle on a per-thread value of 0.00125, giving 1% at 8 threads and 0.125% at 1 thread. Time to rerun the sweep with this adjustment and keep moving efficiently.\n\n","time":{"start":1793011100600,"end":1793011107295},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"tool_use","timestamp":1793011177481,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"type":"tool","tool":"bash","callID":"toolu_01NRqgPXNCj8hcf4RJvRvhxy","state":{"status":"completed","input":{"command":"cd /home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/floydwarshall_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_hybrid_r2/floydwarshall && python3 - <<'EOF'\np='floydwarshall.cpp'; s=open(p).read()\ndef rep(old,new):\n    global s\n    assert s.count(old)==1, old\n    s=s.replace(old,new)\nrep('''// Fraction of each rank's local columns updated by OpenMP host threads.\n// The remaining columns are updated on the rank's GPU.\nconstexpr double CPU_COLUMN_SHARE = 0.01;\n''','''// Fraction of each rank's local columns updated by OpenMP host threads, per host\n// thread. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793011186615,"sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","part":{"id":"prt_177cb605f00187A5QmKlvBHSGb","messageID":"msg_177cb57f7001rBqtdrtgbUnSA8","sessionID":"ses_e884c8cf8ffelzqmk14ntkntw5","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm looking at the scaling numbers and seeing poor efficiency at np=4, only 1.6x speedup at 4096 rows instead of near-4x. I suspect the bottleneck is per-iteration overhead from broadcast and synchronization costs eating into the reduced per-GPU compute time.\n\nQuantifying it, np=1 does roughly 126 G elem/s of raw compute per k, while np=4 should only need ~33us of actual GPU work per k but the overhead per iteration seems to be around 50us, dominated by the sequential D2H, MPI_Bcast, and H2D chain. I'm wondering if there's a way to avoid that sequential dependency, maybe by overlapping the owner's column transfer with other work, though a true fix would need keeping updates accessible without a full device-to-host round trip each iteration.\n\nA cheap, low-risk fix worth trying: switch the host-side column buffer from pageable memory to pinned memory via cudaMallocHost, since DMA transfers are faster and avoid staging overhead. I'll implement that change and measure whether it actually reduces the per-iteration latency before committing to it.\n\n","time":{"start":1793011179615,"end":1793011186559},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
